title: Midnight Blizzard
note: Facts come from the sources below. Evidence rows are recreated for training and are labelled so in the game. Text in backticks is shown as code. Review before publishing.

sources.title: MSRC: Microsoft Actions Following Attack by Nation State Actor Midnight Blizzard (Jan 19, 2024)
Microsoft Security Blog: Midnight Blizzard guidance for responders (Jan 25, 2024)
Microsoft Security Insider: Midnight Blizzard threat actor profile

blocks.text: Microsoft's security team has detected a nation-state attacker inside its corporate email. Senior leaders' mailboxes have been read.
Everything in this case comes from Microsoft's own published investigation. Log entries in the game are recreated for training.

kv.v: Attributed by the US and UK governments to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR)
Quiet: misused legitimate sign-ins and app permissions.

blocks.text: There is no virus to find. The attacker used normal sign-ins and normal app permissions. Your job is to spot legitimate features being misused, which is the hardest kind of attack to see.

items.t: A very small percentage of corporate mailboxes were accessed, including
Attacker's access investigated, disrupted and removed.

blocks.text: Two separate Microsoft tenants. A forgotten test environment had a hidden bridge into the real one.

flow.arrow: ▼ hidden bridge: app had access to the corporate tenant

flow.teaser: ? What happened next is in the evidence

items.t: put the evidence in order and find patient zero.
Rewind to October 2023, before the attacker got in. Deploy controls on a budget and replay the real attack.

blocks.small: Stars: stop it early, waste nothing on decoys, keep users happy.

threatActor.v: Midnight Blizzard (Microsoft's name; also tracked as APT29)

act1.title: Rebuild the timeline
act1.short: Put the evidence in the order it happened. Red herrings go to Not related.
act1.help: Drag an evidence card onto the timeline in the order it happened, or onto Not related. You can also tap a card, then use the buttons.
act1.pzHelp: Tap the timeline entry that shows the first successful access.
act1.doneHelp: Seven steps from a forgotten test account to senior leadership's inboxes.
act1.finding: Patient zero was svc-test, a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. The spray used only a few tries per account across a limited number of accounts, so lockouts never fired. From there, an over-privileged test app became the bridge into the corporate tenant.

hints.1: Look for many sign-in failures spread thinly across accounts.
hints.2: Which log shows the first time they actually got in?
hints.3: Once inside the test tenant, which over-privileged identity did they use next?
hints.4: Next they built their own tools.
hints.5: Someone had to approve those new apps.

wrongLines.early: Not yet. Something else had to happen before this.
wrongLines.pz: That is not the first successful access.

evidence.title: A limited set of accounts, 1–2 failed sign-ins each, from many home IP addresses
Sign-in success: svc-test (legacy test tenant), MFA not required
Legacy-Test-App, a legacy test OAuth app with elevated access to the corporate tenant, is now acting for the attacker
New user created in the corporate tenant → consent granted to the new apps
App role assigned: `full_access_as_app` (Office 365 Exchange Online)

timeline.text: Password spray against a limited number of accounts, from residential proxies, with a low number of attempts.
timeline.why: Few tries per account stayed under lockout and detection thresholds.

timeline.text: Compromised a legacy, non-production test tenant account.
timeline.why: The account had no MFA, so one guessed password was enough.

timeline.text: Used a legacy test OAuth application that had elevated access to the Microsoft corporate environment.
timeline.why: An old app still held standing privilege. Microsoft has not said how the attacker gained control of it.
More apps meant more ways back in if one was found.

timeline.text: Created a new user account to grant consent in the corporate environment to the actor-controlled apps.
timeline.why: Consent turned the attacker's apps into trusted apps.

timeline.text: Used the legacy test app to grant the Office 365 Exchange Online `full_access_as_app` role.
timeline.why: One app role unlocked mailbox access without any user signing in.

timeline.text: Accessed a very small percentage of corporate email accounts, including senior leadership, cybersecurity and legal, and searched for information about Midnight Blizzard itself.
timeline.why: App-only access looked like normal app traffic. Detected 12 Jan 2024, disclosed 19 Jan 2024.

rewind: Now rewind. You're Microsoft's security team in October 2023. Stop it.

links.test: ▼ hidden bridge into the corporate tenant

stages.name: Guessed password works on the test account

map.note: ATT&CK codes for each stage come from the timeline above, so Act 1 and Act 2 always match.

hidden.name: Legacy, non-production test tenant account · no MFA

controls.name: Conditional Access: require MFA in the production tenant
controls.whyScoped: Covered the production tenant only. The sprayed account lived in a legacy test tenant outside the policy.
controls.teach: A policy only protects what's in its scope.

controls.name: Inventory non-production tenants
controls.why: Found it: a legacy, non-production test tenant account with no MFA.
controls.teach: You can't protect what you haven't found.

controls.name: Require MFA in the test tenant too
controls.why: Spray found the password, but MFA stopped the login.
controls.teach: Test tenants are real attack surface.

controls.name: Decommission the legacy test tenant
controls.why: No forgotten test tenant, no target.

controls.name: ID Protection risk policy
controls.why: Risky sign-in flagged. SOC alerted early.

controls.name: Least privilege for apps
controls.why: Test app had no right to grant mailbox access.

controls.name: Admin consent only
controls.why: Consent needed approval. Apps never authorized.

controls.name: OAuth app governance alerts
controls.why: New high-privilege apps raised an alert.

controls.name: Scope app mailbox access
controls.why: The app could reach only the mailboxes it was scoped to, and leadership mailboxes weren't in scope.

controls.name: Alert on unusual EWS access
controls.why: Mass mailbox reading by an app detected.

controls.name: Rehearsed IR runbook: revoke app access fast
controls.why: Your team can cut the attacker's apps off and rotate credentials quickly.
controls.teach: Recovery is a layer too: plan the way back.

controls.name: Lockout after 3 tries
controls.why: Spray used only 1–2 tries per account. Lockout never fired.

controls.name: Geo-block Russia
controls.why: Residential proxies looked like normal local traffic.

controls.name: Password change every 30 days
controls.why: Spray targets common passwords, not old ones.

controls.name: Endpoint antivirus upgrade
controls.why: No malware involved. All cloud identity.

controls.name: Perimeter firewall rule
controls.why: No network perimeter crossed. All cloud sign-ins.

stars.two: stopped at the entry stage (damage NONE). That needs every way in discovered first.
stars.three: ★★ plus at least one detect and one recover control in the build
stars.nextOne: ★: stop the attack at any stage.
stars.nextTwo: ★★: stop it at the entry stage. Find every way in before you lock the door.
stars.nextThree: ★★★: add a detect and a recover layer in case prevention fails.

act2.title: Harden the tenant
act2.short: October 2023. Deploy controls on a budget, then run the real attack against your build.
act2.help: Tap a control to deploy or remove it, or drag it onto a stage in the zone it protects. Each control costs energy and the budget is 9, so you can't buy everything. Not every asset is in your inventory yet: discovery controls find what's missing. Then execute the attack: it replays stage by stage against your build, and the log explains every result.

prevented.title: Breach prevented
prevented.sub: Attack chain broken at stage {n} of {total}. They never got in.

contained.title: Breach contained
contained.sub: They got in, but you stopped them at stage {n} of {total}, before the mailboxes.

detected.title: Breach detected
detected.sub: They reached the mailboxes, but your detection caught them in progress.

succeeded.title: Breach succeeded
succeeded.sub: Like the real incident: weeks of mailbox access before anyone noticed.

tips.notStopped: The attack ran all the way. Check where it really got in, and whether that account was in your inventory.
tips.unknownAsset: The attacker entered via an asset not in your inventory. You can't protect what you haven't found.
tips.notEntry: Stopped, but only after they got in. For ★★, stop it at the entry stage.
tips.needLayers: Prevention held. For ★★★, add a detect and a recover layer in case it fails next time.
tips.decoys: {n} decoy(s) cost budget but did nothing against this attack.
tips.friction: High friction: users will push back. Find a lighter build.
tips.always: Microsoft's Jan 25 guidance covers two areas: protecting against password spray, and defending against malicious OAuth apps by auditing privileged apps, consent and mailbox access.

logs.overBudget: [!] over budget: {name} costs {cost}, you have {left} left. Remove a control first.
